reference_title: Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design - Part 2: Ground investigation and testing

sections.title: Objectives
sections.summary: Heading for the objectives of ground investigations: general (2.1.1), ground (2.1.2), construction materials (2.1.3) and groundwater (2.1.4).
sections.body: Heading for 2.1.1 to 2.1.4; it has no text of its own. (p. 20)
sections.applicability: Governs the overall planning philosophy for any ground investigation programme and directs the choice of sampling/test method by the type of information sought.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Investigations must supply relevant information at each project stage, adequate to manage identified risks, covering ground, geology, geomorphology, seismicity, hydrology and variability. A desk study (maps, photos, previous investigations, local experience) and a site inspection precede the programme, which is reviewed as results arrive; quality assurance applies throughout.
sections.body: (1)P Investigations shall be planned so relevant information is available at each project stage, adequate to manage identified and anticipated risks, including accidents, delays and damage during building stages. (2) They aim to establish soil, rock and groundwater conditions, determine soil and rock properties and gather other site knowledge. (3)P Information on ground conditions, geology, geomorphology, seismicity and hydrology shall be carefully collected, recorded and interpreted, taking account of ground variability. (4) Conditions that may affect the geotechnical category should be found early; NOTE: the investigations may show the category needs changing. (5) Investigations include ground investigations and others such as appraisal of existing constructions and the site's development history. (6) A desk study precedes programme design; (7) sources include topographical, old city, geological, engineering geological, hydrogeological and geotechnical maps, aerial photos, aero-geophysics, previous investigations, local experience and climate (p. 20). (8) Ground investigations comprise field investigations, laboratory testing, further desk studies and controlling and monitoring. (9)P The site shall be visually examined, recorded and cross-checked against the desk study before the programme is drawn up. (10) The programme is reviewed as results arrive: add investigation points for complex or variable ground, check parameters for consistent behaviour, and consider data limitations (EN 1997-1, 3.4.3 (1)). (11) Previously used sites need special attention. (12)P Quality assurance shall be in place in laboratory, field and office, with competent quality control in all phases (p. 21). (pp. 20 to 21)
key_points: Information shall be adequate to manage identified and anticipated project risks (p. 20).
Ground variability shall be taken into account (p. 20).
Find conditions affecting the geotechnical category as early as possible (p. 20).
A desk study precedes the investigation programme (p. 20).
The site shall be visually examined before the programme is drawn up (p. 21).
Review the programme as results become available; add points where ground is variable (p. 21).
Quality assurance in laboratory, field and office (p. 21).
sections.applicability: Governs the overall planning philosophy for any ground investigation programme and directs the choice of sampling/test method by the type of information sought.

sections.title: Ground
sections.summary: Ground investigations shall describe ground conditions and give a basis for parameters at all construction stages, enabling assessment of site suitability and risk, deformations, limit states, ground loads on the structure, foundation methods and sequence, effects on surroundings, extra structural measures and contamination.
sections.body: (1)P Ground investigations shall describe the ground conditions relevant to the works and give a basis for assessing geotechnical parameters for all construction stages. (2) The information should, if possible, allow assessment of: site suitability and acceptable risk; ground deformation from the structure or construction, its distribution and behaviour over time; safety against limit states (subsidence, heave, uplift, slippage, pile buckling); loads from the ground on the structure (e.g. lateral pressures on piles); foundation methods (ground improvement, excavatability, pile driveability, drainage); sequence of foundation works; effects of the structure and of construction on the surroundings; additional measures (excavation support, anchorage, sleeving of bored piles, removal of obstructions); and the type and extent of contamination and the effectiveness of containment or remediation. (p. 21)
key_points: Ground investigations give a basis for parameters at all construction stages (p. 21).
Assess deformation over time, limit states, ground loads, foundation methods and contamination (p. 21).
sections.applicability: Governs the overall planning philosophy for any ground investigation programme and directs the choice of sampling/test method by the type of information sought.

sections.title: Construction materials
sections.summary: Investigations of soil and rock as construction materials shall describe them and set their parameters, assessing suitability, deposit extent, extraction and processing, improvement, workability and property changes, construction traffic effects, dewatering and excavation, weathering, shrinkage, swelling and disintegration.
sections.body: (1)P Investigations of soil and rock for use as construction materials shall describe the materials and establish their parameters. (2) The information should allow assessment of suitability for the intended use; extent of deposits; whether extraction and processing are possible and how unsuitable material is separated and disposed of; improvement methods; workability and property changes during transport, placement and treatment; effects of construction traffic and heavy loads; and dewatering or excavation methods, effects of precipitation, weathering resistance and susceptibility to shrinkage, swelling and disintegration. (p. 22)
key_points: Assess suitability, extent, workability and property changes of material deposits (p. 22).
Assess susceptibility to shrinkage, swelling and disintegration (p. 22).
sections.applicability: Governs the overall planning philosophy for any ground investigation programme and directs the choice of sampling/test method by the type of information sought.

sections.title: Groundwater
sections.summary: Groundwater investigations shall give all information needed for design and construction: water-bearing strata and rock joints, groundwater and piezometric levels with variation and extremes, pore pressures, chemistry and temperature, to assess lowering, harmful effects on excavations and slopes, protection, effects on surroundings, absorption capacity and use of local water.
sections.body: (1)P Groundwater investigations shall provide all relevant groundwater information for design and construction. (2) When appropriate: depth, thickness, extent and permeability of water-bearing strata and rock joint systems; groundwater or piezometric levels, their variation over time, actual levels and possible extremes with return periods; pore water pressure distribution; chemical composition and temperature. (3) Enough to assess, where relevant: scope and nature of groundwater lowering; harmful effects on excavations or slopes (hydraulic failure, seepage pressure, erosion); protective measures (waterproofing, drainage, aggressive water); effects of lowering, desiccation or impounding on the surroundings; the ground's capacity to absorb injected water; and whether local groundwater can be used for construction given its chemistry. (p. 22)
key_points: Include groundwater level variation over time and possible extreme levels with return periods (p. 22).
Assess risk of hydraulic failure, seepage pressure or erosion in excavations and slopes (p. 22).
Include groundwater chemistry and temperature (p. 22).
sections.applicability: Governs the overall planning philosophy for any ground investigation programme and directs the choice of sampling/test method by the type of information sought.

sections.title: Sequence of ground investigations
sections.summary: Investigation scope follows the anticipated construction, foundation, improvement or retaining type, location and depth, with points targeted at ground variation after the desk study and site inspection. Investigations normally run in phases (preliminary 2.3, design 2.4, controlling and monitoring 2.5), each phase's results available before the next; if done at once, 2.3 and 2.4 apply together.
sections.body: (1)P The composition and extent of ground investigations shall be based on the anticipated type and design of construction, foundation, improvement method or retaining structure, and its location and depth (p. 22). (2)P Desk study and site inspection results shall be considered in choosing methods and locating points, targeted at the variation in soil, rock and groundwater conditions. (3) Investigations should normally be phased: preliminary (2.3), design (2.4), controlling and monitoring (2.5); NOTE: the provisions assume one phase's results are available before the next starts. (4) Where all investigations are done at once, 2.3 and 2.4 should be considered together; NOTE: stages can follow the schemes in B.1 and B.2 (p. 23). (pp. 22 to 23)
key_points: Scope based on the anticipated construction type, foundation, location and depth (p. 22).
Target investigation points at the variation in ground conditions (p. 23).
Phases: preliminary, design, controlling and monitoring (p. 23).
If all investigations are done at once, apply 2.3 and 2.4 together (p. 23).
sections.applicability: Establishes the phased structure (preliminary -> design -> monitoring) that the rest of Section 2 elaborates.

sections.title: Preliminary investigations
sections.summary: Preliminary investigations assess overall stability and suitability, compare alternative sites, position the structure, evaluate effects on neighbours, identify borrow areas, consider foundation and improvement methods and plan the design investigations, estimating soil type and stratification, groundwater, preliminary strength and deformation properties and contamination.
sections.body: (1) Preliminary investigations should give data, if relevant, to assess overall stability and general suitability, compare alternative sites, position the structure, evaluate effects on neighbouring buildings and sites, identify borrow areas, consider foundation methods and ground improvement, and plan design and control investigations including the extent of ground influencing the structure. (2) They should estimate, if relevant: soil or rock type and stratification; groundwater table or pore pressure profile; preliminary strength and deformation properties; and potential contamination hazardous to construction materials. (p. 23)
key_points: Assess overall stability, site suitability and positioning of the structure (p. 23).
Estimate stratification, groundwater and preliminary strength and deformation properties (p. 23).
Plan the design investigations, including the extent of influencing ground (p. 23).
sections.applicability: First phase of ground investigation: coarse-grained feasibility and site-suitability assessment ahead of detailed design investigations.

sections.title: Design investigations
sections.summary: Heading for design investigations: field investigations (2.4.1) and laboratory tests (2.4.2).
sections.body: Heading for 2.4.1 and 2.4.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 24)
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Field investigations
sections.summary: Heading for the field investigations of the design phase: general (2.4.1.1), programme (2.4.1.2), locations and depths (2.4.1.3), sampling (2.4.1.4) and groundwater (2.4.1.5).
sections.body: Heading for 2.4.1.1 to 2.4.1.5; it has no text of its own. (p. 24)
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Design-phase field investigations complement the preliminary ones: drilling or excavation for sampling, groundwater measurements and field tests (CPT, SPT, DP, WST, PMT, DMT, PLT, FVT, permeability), plus geophysics and large-scale tests. Table 2.1 guides the applicability of the Section 3 and 4 methods by ground type; contamination or soil gas is gathered beforehand and reported if found.
sections.body: (1)P Where the preliminary investigations do not give what 2.3 needs, complementary investigations shall be made in the design phase. (2) If relevant, design-phase field investigations comprise drilling and/or excavations (test pits, shafts, headings) for sampling, groundwater measurements and field tests. (3) Examples: field tests (CPT, SPT, dynamic probing, WST, pressuremeter, dilatometer, plate load, field vane and permeability tests); soil and rock sampling for description and laboratory tests; groundwater measurements for the water table or pore pressure profile and their fluctuations; geophysics (seismic profiling, ground penetrating radar, resistivity, down-hole logging); large-scale tests, e.g. on prototype elements such as anchors. (4) Table 2.1 can guide planning by the applicability of the field methods of Sections 3 and 4. (5)P Where contamination or soil gas is expected, information shall be gathered from the relevant sources and used in planning (p. 24). Table 2.1 rates applicability as C1 to C3 for coarse soil, F1 to F3 for fine soil and R1 to R3 for rock (high, medium, low): the applicability of sampling methods, field tests and groundwater measurements for basic information (type of soil or rock, extension of layers, groundwater level, pore water pressure) and geotechnical properties (particle size, water content, Atterberg limits, density, shear strength, compressibility, permeability, chemical tests); the selection may deviate with ground conditions and design (p. 25). (6)P Contamination or soil gas detected during the investigations shall be reported to the client and the responsible authorities (p. 26). (pp. 24 to 26)
key_points: Complementary investigations in the design phase where the preliminary ones fall short (p. 24).
Field investigations: sampling by drilling or excavation, groundwater measurements, field tests (p. 24).
Table 2.1 rates applicability for coarse soil, fine soil and rock (high, medium, low) (p. 25).
Detected contamination or soil gas shall be reported to the client and authorities (p. 26).

sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Field investigation programme
sections.summary: The field investigation programme shall contain a plan of investigation point locations and types, depths, sample types (category, number, depths), groundwater measurement specifications, equipment and the standards applied.
sections.body: (1)P The field investigation programme shall contain: a plan of the investigation point locations with the types of investigation; the depth of investigation; the types of sample (category etc.) with their number and depths; specifications for groundwater measurement; the equipment types; and the standards to apply. (p. 26)
key_points: Programme lists locations, depths, sample categories, groundwater measurements, equipment, standards (p. 26).
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Locations and depths of the investigation points
sections.summary: Point locations and depths follow the preliminary investigations, geology, structure size and problems: patterns that show stratification, critical points (e.g. foundation corners), offsets for linear structures, points beyond slopes and cuts, no hazard to works, coverage of neighbouring ground. Uniform or strong ground may justify fewer points by local experience; CPTs before boreholes, at least 2 m apart if drilled first.
sections.body: (1)P Locations and depths shall follow from the preliminary investigations, geology, structure dimensions and engineering problems. (2) Arrange points so stratification can be assessed across the site; place them at critical points for shape, behaviour and loads (e.g. foundation corners); for linear structures at offsets from the centre line suited to the width; for structures on or near slopes and steps also outside the project area, so slope or cut stability can be assessed, considering anchor load transfer zones; so they pose no hazard to the structure, works or surroundings (changes to ground and groundwater); extending into neighbouring ground until no harmful influence is expected; and consider keeping groundwater points for monitoring during and after construction (p. 26). (3) Relatively uniform ground, or ground known to be strong and stiff enough, may justify wider spacing or fewer points, justified by local experience. (4)P Different investigation types at one location (e.g. CPT and piston sampling) shall be separated by an appropriate distance. (5) With CPTs and boreholes, do the CPTs first, spaced so the borehole is unlikely to meet the CPT hole; if drilling comes first, the CPT should be at least 2 m away horizontally. (6)P Depths shall reach all strata affecting or affected by the project; for dams, weirs, excavations below groundwater and dewatering they also depend on hydrogeology; slopes and steps shall be explored below any potential slip surface. NOTE: B.3 gives guidance values for spacing and depths (p. 27). (pp. 26 to 27)
key_points: Locations and depths follow preliminary investigations, geology, structure size and problems (p. 26).
Place points at critical locations such as foundation corners (p. 26).
Wider spacing in uniform or strong ground only if justified by local experience (p. 27).
Do CPTs before boreholes; a CPT after drilling at least 2 m away horizontally (p. 27).
Explore slopes and steps below any potential slip surface (p. 27).
Annex B.3 gives guidance on spacing and depths (p. 27).
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Sampling
sections.summary: Sampling categories (3.4.1, 3.5.1) and numbers follow the investigation aim, geology and complexity; at least one borehole or trial pit with sampling is needed, sampling every layer affecting the structure. Field tests may replace sampling only with enough local experience for unambiguous correlation.
sections.body: (1)P Sampling categories (3.4.1 and 3.5.1) and numbers of samples shall follow the aim of the investigation, site geology and complexity of the geotechnical structure. (2)P At least one borehole or trial pit with sampling shall be available for identification and classification, with samples from every separate layer influencing the structure. (3) Field tests may replace sampling where local experience allows unambiguous correlation with ground conditions. (4) Section 3 gives details. (p. 27)
key_points: At least one borehole or trial pit with sampling for identification and classification (p. 27).
Sample every separate layer influencing the structure (p. 27).
Field tests may replace sampling only with sufficient local experience (p. 27).
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Groundwater
sections.summary: Groundwater measurements in the design phase shall be planned and carried out according to 3.6, the groundwater measurement clauses of Section 3.
sections.body: (1)P Groundwater measurements shall be planned and carried out in accordance with 3.6. (p. 27)
key_points: Groundwater measurements per 3.6 (p. 27).
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Laboratory tests
sections.summary: Heading for laboratory tests in the design phase: general, visual inspection, test programme, number of tests, classification tests and tests on samples (2.4.2.1 to 2.4.2.6).
sections.body: Heading for 2.4.2.1 to 2.4.2.6; it has no text of its own. (p. 27)
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Before setting up the test programme, establish the expected stratigraphy and select design-relevant strata to specify test types and numbers per stratum, by problem, complexity, geology and required parameters.
sections.body: (1) Before the test programme is set up, the expected stratigraphy should be established and the strata relevant for design selected so the type and number of tests in each can be specified; stratum identification depends on the geotechnical problem, its complexity, local geology and the parameters needed. (p. 27)
key_points: Establish expected stratigraphy and design-relevant strata before the test programme (p. 27).
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Visual inspection and preliminary ground profile
sections.summary: Samples and trial pits are inspected visually against drilling logs to set a preliminary ground profile, with simple manual tests for soil; strata with distinct differences are subdivided; sample quality (Table 3.1 classes) is assessed before testing where practicable.
sections.body: (1) Samples and trial pits should be inspected visually and compared with the field logs to establish the preliminary ground profile, soil samples supported by simple manual tests of identity, consistency and behaviour. (2) Distinct, significant differences within a stratum call for subdividing the profile (p. 27). (3) Where practicable, sample quality should be assessed before laboratory testing; soil sample quality classes are in Table 3.1 (p. 28). (pp. 27 to 28)
key_points: Compare samples with field logs to build a preliminary ground profile (p. 27).
Subdivide strata with distinct, significant property differences (p. 27).
Assess sample quality (Table 3.1 classes) before laboratory tests where practicable (p. 28).
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Test programme
sections.summary: The laboratory programme follows construction type, ground and stratigraphy and the design parameters, and the extent of comparable experience and observations on neighbouring structures. Specimens must represent their strata, checked by classification tests, iteratively; more advanced tests or investigation are considered as the project, soil and model require.
sections.body: (1)P The laboratory programme shall take account of the construction type, ground type and stratigraphy and the parameters needed for design. (2) It depends partly on comparable experience, whose extent and quality for the soil or rock should be established; observations on neighbouring structures should be used where available. (3)P Tests shall be on specimens representative of the relevant strata, checked by classification tests; NOTE: iteratively, first classification and index tests on as many samples as possible to find the range of index properties, then comparing the strength and compressibility specimens' classification and strength index results with those of the whole stratum. (4) The need for more advanced testing or further investigation should be considered by project aspects, soil type and variability and the computation model. (p. 28)
key_points: Programme follows construction type, stratigraphy and design parameters (p. 28).
Establish the extent and quality of comparable experience (p. 28).
Specimens shall represent their strata, checked by classification tests (p. 28).
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Number of tests
sections.summary: Specimen numbers depend on ground homogeneity, comparable experience and geotechnical category, with spares for difficult soil or damage and a minimum per test type (recommended in Annexes L to W). Fewer tests are acceptable with conservative parameters, no optimisation, or comparable experience and field data.
sections.body: (1)P The number of specimens shall depend on ground homogeneity, the quality and amount of comparable experience and the geotechnical category. (2) Extra specimens should be available for difficult soil, damaged specimens and other factors. (3) A minimum number should be tested per test type; NOTE: recommended minimums for some tests are in the tables of Annexes L to W, which also help check whether the investigation was sufficient. (4) The minimum may be reduced if the design need not be optimised and uses conservative parameters, or with comparable experience or field information. (p. 28)
key_points: Specimen numbers depend on homogeneity, comparable experience and geotechnical category (p. 28).
Recommended minimum numbers of tests are tabulated in Annexes L to W (p. 28).
Minimums may be reduced with conservative parameters or comparable experience (p. 28).
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Classification tests
sections.summary: Classification tests find each stratum's composition and index properties, spread evenly over the area and full depth of design-relevant strata to show their range, and check whether a second investigation stage is needed; Table 2.2 lists routine tests by sample disturbance.
sections.body: (1) Classification tests should determine the composition and index properties of each stratum, with samples distributed roughly evenly over the whole area and full depth of the design-relevant strata, so the results show the range of index properties (p. 28). (2) The results should be used to check whether the investigation was sufficient or a second stage is needed. (3) Table 2.2 gives suitable routine classification tests for samples of various disturbance, generally performed in all phases (2.2 (3)) (p. 29). (pp. 28 to 29)
key_points: Spread classification samples over the full area and depth of relevant strata (p. 28).
Use classification results to judge whether a second investigation stage is needed (p. 29).
sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Tests on samples
sections.summary: Test samples cover each stratum's range of index properties; fills and sands or gravels may use reconstituted specimens matching in-situ composition, density and water content. Table 2.2 lists soil classification tests, Table 2.3 laboratory tests for parameters; rock: geological classification, density, water content, porosity, UCS, E and Poisson's ratio, point load index, core logging with RQD.
sections.body: (1)P Samples shall cover the range of index properties of each relevant stratum. (2) For fill or sand or gravel strata, reconstituted specimens of about the in-situ composition, density and water content may be tested (p. 29). Table 2.2 lists soil classification tests by soil type and sample disturbance (some results possible to determine but not necessarily representative); further tests such as organic content, particle density and activity may be considered. (3) Laboratory tests for parameters for geotechnical calculations are in Table 2.3. (4) Routine rock tests: geological classification, density or bulk mass density, water content, porosity, uniaxial compression strength, Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio, and point load strength index Is(50). (5) Rock core classification normally comprises geological description, core recovery, RQD, induration, fracture log, weathering and fissuring; other tests may include grain density, wave velocity, Brazilian, rock and joint shear strength, slake durability, swelling and abrasion tests (p. 30). (6) Rock mass properties may be studied indirectly by compression and shear tests along joints, and in weak rocks by field or large-scale block tests. Table 2.3 gives the laboratory tests for each geotechnical parameter by soil type (bracketed entries only partially applicable; see Section 5) (p. 31). (pp. 29 to 31)
key_points: Test samples shall cover each stratum's range of index properties (p. 29).
Reconstituted specimens allowed for fill, sand or gravel strata (p. 29).
Routine rock tests include UCS, E and Poisson's ratio and point load index Is(50) (p. 30).
Rock core classification includes core recovery and RQD (p. 30).

sections.title: Controlling and monitoring
sections.summary: During construction, checks and tests confirm the ground matches the design investigations and materials and works match assumptions: ground profile checks in excavation and inspection of excavation bottoms are required; groundwater, neighbouring and actual construction behaviour may be measured, vital for the observational method; results are reported, checked and acted on.
sections.body: (1)P Checks and additional tests shall be made during construction and execution, when relevant, to confirm the ground agrees with the design investigations and that delivered materials and works match what was presumed or specified (EN 1997-1:2004, Section 4) (p. 31). (2)P Required: checking the ground profile when excavating and inspecting the bottom of the excavation. (3) Optional general measures: groundwater level or pore pressure measurements and fluctuations; behaviour of neighbouring constructions, services or works; and behaviour of the construction itself; NOTE: controlling and monitoring are of prime importance with the observational method. (4)P Results shall be compiled, reported and checked against the design requirements, and decisions taken on them (p. 32). (pp. 31 to 32)
key_points: Check the ground profile when excavating and inspect the excavation bottom (p. 31).
Monitoring is of prime importance when the observational method is used (p. 32).
Control results shall be reported, checked against design and acted on (p. 32).
sections.applicability: Post-design-phase verification of ground behaviour against the assumptions used in design.
